title: Anatomy Overview
shortDescription: What anatomy and physiology actually study, the levels of body organization, and the major organ systems — the map before the territory.
genZNote: Before you learn any organ by name, learn the zoom levels the body is built at.

sections.heading: Anatomy vs. Physiology
sections.body:
Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body and the relationships between its parts — what things look like, where they sit, and how they're built. Physiology is the study of function — how those structures actually work and keep the body alive.

The two are always taught together because structure and function are inseparable: the shape of the small intestine (long, folded, lined with villi) exists because of what it needs to do (absorb nutrients).
bullets: Anatomy = structure ("what is it, where is it").
Physiology = function ("what does it do, how does it work").
Gross anatomy studies structures visible to the naked eye; microscopic anatomy (histology) studies tissues and cells under a microscope.

sections.heading: Levels of Structural Organization
sections.body: The human body is organized into a hierarchy, from the simplest to the most complex level. Each level builds on the one below it.

steps.name: Chemical level
steps.explanation: Atoms combine to form molecules (e.g. water, proteins, DNA).
steps.purpose: The basic chemical building blocks of everything alive.

steps.name: Cellular level
steps.explanation: Molecules combine to form cells — the smallest unit of life.
steps.purpose: Cells carry out the basic functions of life (metabolism, reproduction, response).

steps.name: Tissue level
steps.explanation: Groups of similar cells performing a common function (epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous tissue).
steps.purpose: Tissues are the working material organs are built from.

steps.name: Organ level
steps.explanation: Two or more tissue types working together for a specific function (e.g. the heart, stomach, kidney).
steps.purpose: Organs perform complex, specific jobs no single tissue could do alone.

steps.name: Organ system level
steps.explanation: Organs that work together for a broader purpose (e.g. the digestive system).
steps.purpose: Systems coordinate multiple organs toward one shared physiological goal.

steps.name: Organism level
steps.explanation: All the organ systems functioning together as one living being.

sections.heading: Anatomical Position and Body Planes
sections.body:
Anatomical position is the universal reference posture used to describe body locations without ambiguity: standing upright, facing forward, feet flat and together, arms at the sides, palms facing forward.

Body planes are imaginary flat surfaces used to section the body for description and imaging.
bullets: Sagittal plane — divides the body into left and right parts.
Midsagittal (median) plane — a sagittal plane exactly down the midline, giving equal left and right halves.
Frontal (coronal) plane — divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) parts.
Transverse (horizontal/axial) plane — divides the body into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) parts.

sections.heading: Body Cavities
sections.body: The body has two main sets of internal cavities that house and protect the organs (viscera).

rows: Heart, lungs, esophagus (split into two pleural cavities + the mediastinum)
Below the diaphragm to the pelvic brim
Stomach, liver, intestines, kidneys, spleen, pancreas
Basin formed by the hip bones

sections.heading: The Major Organ Systems
bullets: Cardiovascular — heart, blood vessels, blood; transports gases, nutrients, hormones, waste.
Respiratory — lungs, airway; gas exchange (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out).
Digestive — GI tract, liver, pancreas; breaks down food, absorbs nutrients.
Nervous — brain, spinal cord, nerves; control and communication.
Skeletal — bones, joints; support, protection, movement, mineral storage.
Muscular — skeletal, smooth, and cardiac muscle; movement and heat production.
Urinary — kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra; waste removal, fluid/electrolyte balance.
Lymphatic/Immune — lymph nodes, spleen, thymus; defense and fluid return.
Reproductive — gonads and associated organs; reproduction.
Integumentary — skin, hair, nails; protection, temperature regulation, sensation.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Anatomy studies body structure, physiology studies body function, and both are organized from the chemical level up to the whole organism.
keyFacts: Six levels of organization: chemical → cellular → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
Anatomical position: standing, facing forward, arms at sides, palms forward.
Three main planes: sagittal (left/right), frontal/coronal (front/back), transverse (upper/lower).
The dorsal (cranial + vertebral) and ventral (thoracic + abdominopelvic) cavities are the two main body cavity groups.
commonConfusion: A sagittal plane divides left/right; a frontal (coronal) plane divides front/back — these two are the most commonly swapped in exams.
"Abdominal cavity" and "pelvic cavity" are often tested as one combined "abdominopelvic cavity" — know both the split and the combined name.

highYieldFacts: There are exactly six levels of structural organization, always given in the same order.
Midsagittal = exact midline; any other left/right cut is just "sagittal" (parasagittal).
commonTraps: Don't confuse anatomy (structure) with physiology (function) when a question asks which term applies to a description of "how" something works.
Transverse plane is horizontal, not vertical — it separates top from bottom, not left from right.
mustRemember: Chemical → Cellular → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism.
Four basic tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.

sources.name: National Cancer Institute SEER Training — Anatomy & Physiology

structures.name: Cell
structures.description: The smallest structural and functional unit of life; the building block every tissue is made from.
structures.function: Carries out metabolism, reproduction, and response to stimuli at the smallest scale of the body.
structures.highYield: Every level above this one (tissue, organ, system) is just cells organized at increasing scale.

structures.name: Tissue
structures.description: A group of similar cells working together for a common function.
structures.function: Four basic types: epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue.
structures.highYield: An organ is never made of one tissue type alone — it's always two or more tissues combined.

structures.name: Organ
structures.description: Two or more tissue types working together for a specific, complex job (e.g. the heart, stomach, kidney).
structures.function: Performs a job no single tissue could do alone.

structures.name: Organ system
structures.description: A group of organs that work together toward one broad physiological goal (e.g. the digestive system).
structures.function: Coordinates multiple organs toward one shared purpose.

pathways.title: Levels of Structural Organization
steps: Chemical level — atoms combine into molecules
Cellular level — molecules combine into cells
Tissue level — cells combine into tissues
Organ level — tissues combine into organs
Organ system level — organs combine into systems
Organism level — all systems function together

comparisons.distinction: Anatomy studies structure (what it is, where it is); physiology studies function (what it does, how it works).
Sagittal divides the body into left and right; frontal divides it into front (anterior) and back (posterior).
Gross anatomy studies structures visible to the naked eye; histology studies tissues and cells under a microscope.

questions.prompt: Which term describes the study of body structure, as opposed to function?
questions.explanation: Anatomy is the study of structure — what a body part is and where it sits. Physiology studies function.
optionNotes: Physiology is the study of function, the opposite pairing.
Histology is the microscopic study of tissues, a sub-field of anatomy, not the general term.
Homeostasis is a stable internal state, a physiological concept, not a field of study.

questions.prompt: Put these in correct order, smallest to largest: Tissue, Organ, Cell, Organ system.
questions.explanation: The hierarchy always runs chemical → cellular → tissue → organ → organ system → organism, so the smallest-to-largest order here is Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system.
optionNotes: Correct — matches the fixed hierarchy of structural organization.
Tissue cannot come before cell — tissues are made of cells.
Organ cannot come before tissue — organs are made of tissues.
Organ cannot come before tissue in the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: True or False: A frontal (coronal) plane divides the body into left and right halves.
questions.explanation: False — that's the sagittal plane. The frontal (coronal) plane divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) parts.
